variants.title: Run both loops
variants.context: Two loops: the knowledge loop ingests sources and publishes an index; the answer loop retrieves candidates, reranks evidence, assembles and answers, then verifies and contains. Identity is preserved across both.
variants.prompt: A RAG system serves one question. Put the loops in order.

items.text: Verify and contain: check policy, support, freshness, citations, latency, and cost before serving.
Rerank evidence: deduplicate, apply metadata and safety filters, spend a bounded second-stage budget.
Ingest sources: discover authorized documents, parse, normalize, attach source and freshness metadata.
Assemble and answer: fit source-labeled evidence into the budget; require claim-linked citations and abstention.
Retrieve candidates: authorize the request before search, encode or rewrite the query, collect candidates.
Publish an index: chunk, compute versioned representations, verify counts, atomically publish one snapshot.

variants.hint: Authorization happens before search, not after.
variants.explanation: Knowledge loop → answer loop, with identity preserved throughout.

variants.prompt: A deleted document must stop appearing. Put the loop stages it touches in order.

items.text: Retrieval no longer returns the chunk.
Verification confirms no citation points at the deleted source.
The index publishes a tombstone in a new snapshot.

variants.hint: Deletion must propagate through every stage.
variants.explanation: Test deletion propagation through storage, queues, replicas, caches, and prompt assembly.

variants.prompt: Latency exceeds budget at verification. Put the answer loop in order, ending with containment.

items.text: Reranking ran within its bounded budget.
Verification finds latency or cost out of contract.
The system degrades, abstains, or routes to review rather than serving late.

variants.hint: Verify and contain is a real stage with its own outcomes.
variants.explanation: Otherwise abstain, degrade, or route to review.

variants.title: Preserve identity
variants.context: Preserve identity: source identity (document, revision, owner, access, effective time), transformation identity (parser, chunker, embedding model, dimensions), index identity (snapshot, metric, filter schema, rollback target), request identity (query, principal, prompt and model versions), evidence identity (chunk IDs, spans, scores, citations shown).
variants.prompt: An operator asks which document revision was searchable when a specific answer was produced. Which identities answer that?
options: Transformation identity alone, since it names the parser and chunker versions.
Index identity with its source checkpoint, joined to the request identity.
Evidence identity alone, since it lists the chunk IDs that were returned.
optionFeedback: Parser and chunker versions say how text was transformed, not which document revision was searchable.
The snapshot and its checkpoint say what was searchable for that request.
Chunk IDs name what came back; the searchable revision set comes from the snapshot checkpoint.
variants.hint: Which record says what was searchable?
variants.explanation: Publish a source checkpoint with the index.

variants.title: Preserve identity
variants.context: Preserve identity: source identity (document, revision, owner, access, effective time), transformation identity (parser, chunker, embedding model, dimensions), index identity (snapshot, metric, filter schema, rollback target), request identity (query, principal, prompt and model versions), evidence identity (chunk IDs, spans, scores, citations shown).
variants.prompt: The chunker changed but the index kept its version. What is the risk?
options: No risk, because the index version already covers every stage of the pipeline.
Indexing gets faster because the new chunker writes fewer records per document.
Evidence units change while transformation identity stays unversioned, so audits cannot be interpreted.
optionFeedback: The index version covers the snapshot, not the chunker. A silent transformation change breaks traceability.
Record count is not the concern. New chunk boundaries change what a piece of evidence means.
Transformation identity must be versioned with the index.
variants.explanation: Version parser, normalizer, tokenizer, chunker, embedding model, and schema.

variants.prompt: Which identity records the citations actually shown to the user?
options: Evidence identity: chunk IDs, source spans, stage scores, and citations shown.
Source identity, which records the document revision, owner, and access policy.
Index identity, which records the snapshot, distance metric, and filter schema.
optionFeedback: Evidence identity captures what the user saw.
Source identity describes which documents were eligible, not which citations were rendered.
Index identity describes what was searchable, not which spans reached the user.
variants.hint: What did the user actually see?
variants.explanation: Evidence identity closes the loop from source to citation.

variants.title: Do the chunk math
variants.context: For fixed token chunks, stride = chunk_tokens − overlap_tokens. Overlap protects boundary facts but repeats embedding work and increases index size and duplicate candidates.
variants.prompt: Chunks are 512 tokens with 64 tokens of overlap. What is the stride?

mistakes.feedback: Subtract the overlap; do not add it.

variants.title: Do the chunk math
variants.context: For fixed token chunks, stride = chunk_tokens − overlap_tokens. Overlap protects boundary facts but repeats embedding work and increases index size and duplicate candidates.
variants.prompt: A 4,480-token document is chunked with a 448-token stride. About how many chunks result?
variants.explanation: 4,480 ÷ 448 = 10 chunks, each carrying some overlap with its neighbor.

mistakes.feedback: Use the stride, not the chunk size.

variants.title: Do the chunk math
variants.context: For fixed token chunks, stride = chunk_tokens − overlap_tokens. Overlap protects boundary facts but repeats embedding work and increases index size and duplicate candidates.
variants.prompt: Chunks are 512 tokens with 64 tokens of overlap. What fraction of tokens in each chunk is duplicated from the previous one, in percent?
variants.explanation: 64 ÷ 512 = 12.5% duplicated tokens; that is repeated embedding work and duplicate candidates.

mistakes.feedback: Express as a percentage of the chunk.

variants.title: Bind the contract
variants.context: Embeddings are meaningful only under the exact representation contract that produced them. Fail closed on dimension, normalization, or metric mismatch; never encode documents with one model and queries with another unless that pairing was trained; re-embed into a new index when the contract changes.
variants.prompt: A query vector has 1,024 dimensions but the index stores 768. What should happen?
options: Fail closed; the contract fingerprints differ.
Truncate the query vector to the first 768 dimensions.
Pad the index vectors with zeros out to 1,024 dimensions.
optionFeedback: Mismatched representations produce meaningless scores.
Truncation invents a mapping between two spaces that was never trained, so the scores mean nothing.
Zero padding changes norms without making the two representations comparable.
variants.hint: Are these vectors in the same space?

variants.title: Bind the contract
variants.context: Embeddings are meaningful only under the exact representation contract that produced them. Fail closed on dimension, normalization, or metric mismatch; never encode documents with one model and queries with another unless that pairing was trained; re-embed into a new index when the contract changes.
variants.prompt: Documents were embedded with model A; to save cost, queries use model B. Is that valid?
options: Yes, as long as both models emit vectors of the same dimension and normalization.
Only if that asymmetric pairing was explicitly trained and evaluated.
Yes, since embedding models train on overlapping web text and land in a shared space.
optionFeedback: Matching dimensions only make the arithmetic run. The two models place meaning in different directions.
Different models produce different spaces.
Shared training data does not produce a shared coordinate system. There is no universal space.
variants.hint: Were these two models trained to share a space?
variants.explanation: Never mix query and document encoders casually.

variants.title: Bind the contract
variants.context: Embeddings are meaningful only under the exact representation contract that produced them. Fail closed on dimension, normalization, or metric mismatch; never encode documents with one model and queries with another unless that pairing was trained; re-embed into a new index when the contract changes.
variants.prompt: The preprocessing changed. What is the release path?
options: Update vectors in place as documents are touched, so the index refreshes gradually.
Nothing, since preprocessing runs before embedding and does not change stored vectors.
Re-embed into a new index, compare recall and latency by slice, then canary the alias.
optionFeedback: A gradual rewrite leaves two representations in one index, so scores stop being comparable.
Preprocessing is part of the representation contract, so changing it changes every vector produced.
Migration evidence protects the serving index.
variants.hint: What happens if old and new vectors coexist?
variants.explanation: Re-embed into a new index when the contract changes; do not silently mix versions.

variants.title: Retrieve, then rank
variants.context: Retrieval finds a broad candidate set; reranking spends more computation on a smaller set. Sparse retrieval for names and identifiers; dense for paraphrases; hybrid fuses both; metadata filtering enforces policy inside the boundary. An average from another corpus is not a local release argument.
variants.prompt: Reranking depth was raised from 20 to 200. What changes?
options: Nothing measurable, because the reranker scores the same candidates either way.
Latency and cost rise directly; precision may improve, but recall does not change.
Recall improves, because the deeper pool gives the reranker more documents to find.
optionFeedback: Depth is the reranker's input size, so scoring ten times more pairs costs real latency.
Reranking only orders what retrieval supplied.
The first stage owns recall. Reranking reorders the candidates retrieval already returned.
variants.explanation: Reranking candidate depth is a direct latency and cost budget.

variants.title: Retrieve, then rank
variants.context: Retrieval finds a broad candidate set; reranking spends more computation on a smaller set. Sparse retrieval for names and identifiers; dense for paraphrases; hybrid fuses both; metadata filtering enforces policy inside the boundary. An average from another corpus is not a local release argument.
variants.prompt: A published benchmark shows dense retrieval beats sparse on average. Is that a local release argument?
options: Yes, if the benchmark is large enough that the average is statistically stable.
No. Measure recall on labeled production-shaped queries first.
Yes, because dense retrieval generalizes across corpora once the encoder is trained.
optionFeedback: Sample size makes the average precise, not local. BEIR showed heterogeneous behavior across tasks.
BEIR showed heterogeneous behavior across tasks.
Dense retrieval still loses to sparse on exact identifiers and rare terms in many corpora.
variants.hint: Whose queries did the benchmark measure?
variants.explanation: Use labeled production-shaped queries to measure recall at candidate depth.

variants.title: Retrieve, then rank
variants.context: Retrieval finds a broad candidate set; reranking spends more computation on a smaller set. Sparse retrieval for names and identifiers; dense for paraphrases; hybrid fuses both; metadata filtering enforces policy inside the boundary. An average from another corpus is not a local release argument.
variants.prompt: Locale and product constraints are applied after reranking as a filter on the final list. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because the same ineligible items are removed either way.
The filters should be dropped so ranking sees the whole corpus and never returns an empty list.
Metadata filtering belongs inside the retrieval boundary, before ranking.
optionFeedback: The rerank budget is spent on candidates that can never be shown, and the final list can empty out.
Locale and product constraints are policy. Dropping them lets ineligible evidence into the answer.
Post-filtering wastes ranking on ineligible items and can empty the result.
variants.explanation: Metadata filtering enforces constraints inside the retrieval boundary.
